The House met at eleven of the clock, Mr. Chairman in the chair, 
THE FIRST ANNIVERSARY OF INDIA'S VICTORY IN KARGIL 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon Members, July 26,2000 marks the first anniversary of 
india's victory in the Kargil conflict when the last of the Pakistani aggressors were 
evicted from our territory. Recalling the sacrifices of many of our brave  soldiers and 
airmen who laid down their lives to protect the territorial integrity of India and the acts 
of courage and gallantry displayed by our troops, this  House saltues the memory of 
those who were k illed in defending the motherland ant. applauds the dedication and 
professional commitment of the members of  our armed forces. This House reaffirms 
the nation's commitment to the welfare of the families of the martyrs and of those who 
were disabled. This House also  recalls, with pride and joy, the great unity, solidarity 
and sense of purpose that  the entire nation displayed during the crisis which 
demonstrated India's unshakeable resolve to foil any misadventure of the kind that our 
neighbour regrettably engaged herself in. 
Today, on the occasion of the Kargil Vijay Diwas, this House reiterates India's 
resolve to beat back any aggression as well as our commitment to the path of peace 
and maintenance of good relations with our neighbours.

Kutir Jyoti Programme for Rural Areas 
†*41. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL:†† 
          DR. D. MASTHAN; 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a programme namely Kutir Jyoti Programme was launched 
to provide electricity in the houses of families living below poverty line in the country, 
particularly in rural and tribal areas; 
(b) if so, the percentage of poor families in rural areas who have been provided with 
electricity under Kutir Jyoti Programme till December 1999; and 
(c) by when the remaining families are likely to be provided with electricity? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMAT1 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Government of India launched Kutir Jyoti Programme in 1988-89 
for extending single point light connection to the households of rural families below 
poverty line including Harijan and Adivasi families. More than

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM): Sir, with your 
permission, I would like to answer. I think the hon. Member if I may submit, I should 
really apologise to him is justified in saying that he had put a very straight question. We 
are revealing the answer. The truth of the matter if that the figure is not very 
complimentary. The total figure is 487.92 lakhs BPL households throughout the country. 
Out of that, we have done only 35 lakhs through our scheme. Though the amount 
involved is Rs. 214.6 crores, the misfortune, perhaps, is that most of these single-light 
connections are connections where meters are not really fixed. In the name of single-
light connection, in many of the cases, more power than a single-light connection is 
actually drawn. The Electricity Boards are relu ctant to use this grant. This is purely a 
grant. They are reluctant to use this grant. We have been pressurising them. In fact, in 
my own home State, I had to pressurise the Electricity Board Chairman to take a little 
more and we are still trying with each other to increase the figure. It is something where we 
need the help of Members of Parliament to make them understand that unless we get our 
households connected with power, there is no use of talking about full electrification. I 
agree with the hon. Member that this is a matter which needs real attention. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: But, at least, the exact figures should be given to us. They 
should be given to me in writing. 
SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM: I will give you the figures.

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2000] 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Sir, the major problem, as stated by Shri Kapil 
Sibal, is it has come down to 3000 in the Ninth Plan. It is not a question of forcing the 
State Electricity Boards. It is because of the new power policy which you have framed. 
The Boards feel that this is absolutely unremunerative. It is unremunerative in the sense 
that you are giving a grant. Up to giving a grant, it is all right. The remuneration is Rs. 
5/- per connection which is becoming totally unremunerative for the Boards. The State 
Government as well as the Central Government  have to decide about the subsidy. This 
has nothing to do with the Boards. Whatever is the target; let us quantify it financially. 
Subsidy is required for the people who cannot pay more than Rs. 5/-. Even tribal areas 
are involved in it. That is why it is not remunerative. Even 50 per cent of the generation 
cost cannot be collected from them. So far as these targeted sections of BPL and tribals 
are concerned, the only decision which we have to take here is, beyond Rs. 5/- 
whatever is the subsidy, let it be shared byboth the State Government and the Central 
Government. If you leave it to the Boards, it will never be possible. You can go on 
forcing them. Can we not decide here as to what is the financial quantification? If you 
really mean business, so far as the BPL people and tribals are concerned, this subsidy 
beyond Rs. 5/- has to be shared by the Central Government and the State Government 
as a poverty alleviation programme, not as a State Electricity Board programme. 
SHRI P.R. KUMARAMANGALAM; Sir, I do agree with the hon. Member. The real 
issue which the Boards are facing is, after giving the connections, as I said earlier, there 
is no income from these connections. Often, a single light  connection becomes not a 
single light connection. Therefore, it is more than calculated system. This is the issue 
which is arising. This is a very genuine issue. In a country which is a developing 
country, there has to be some transparent subsidy available for the weaker sections of 
the society. Now, in certain States, they have prioritised it differently. For example, in 
my State, it is for agriculture and also, by the way, for single light connection. In some 
States, they don't do it. Insofar as Centre's contribution is concerned, we are actually 
giving subsidy by indirect methods. But I think it is much better to look at these things 
transparently. The suggestion of the hon. Member would be looked at very seriously. 
We have a group of Ministers within the Ministry of Rural Electrification, because even 
in rural electrification, getting wire from an urban area or, may be from the main grid into 
a village is uneconomic. Even in UP, it costs Rs. 5-6 lakhs a village; and that village 
does not generate the

†*42.   SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN:†† 
             SHRI V.V.RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to stale: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item as appeared 
in 'The Hindustan Times' dated the 8th June, 2000, under the caption "Christian School 
Principal murdered near Mathura"; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) how many such incidents on attack on Christian minority run institutions have 
taken place in Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat and Orissa during the year 2000 so far and 
Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI I. 
D. SWAMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As per available information, from the Government of Uttar Pradesh, Brother 
George, a warden of St. Francis School (earlier known as Brother Pauls's Memorial 
School) Hostel at Navada under Narhouli Police Station, Mathura was attacked and 
killed by 6-7 assailants on the night of 6th-7th June, 2000, while he was asleep in the 
hostel compound. A case under Section 396 of the IPC was registered at the Narhouli 
Police Station. The matter was handed over to the Crime Branch of the State Police and 
a judicial Inquiry has also been ordered by the State Government under a one-man 
Commission headed by a sitting Judge of the Allahabad High Court. 
(c) As per available information, six incidents have been reported on minority run 
institutions in Uttar Pradesh during this year. No such incidents have been reported in 
this regard from the States of Gujarat and Orissa. 
Besides sharing intelligence inputs, sending advisories from time to time, another 
advisory has been sent to all States/UTs on 19-6-2000, and a high-level meeting, 
consisting of Home Secretaries, DGPs/IGs of Andhra Pradesh, U.P., Karnataka, Goa, 
Orissa and Gujarat, was convened on 4-7-2000 to review the situation, and the State 
Government have been asked to provide security to the minorities and their institutions 
and to deal firmly with the perpetrators of violence against them.

Discussions on security issues with Israel 
399. SHRI C. M. IBRAHIM: W ill the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether during his recent visit to Israel, he discussed security aspects, 
especially the need to counter terrorism as a global menace and counter intelligence 
measures;

(c) how it has affected India's relation with Middle-East, Arab and Gulf countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI CH. 
VIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) to (c) During the recent visit to Israel, we 
interacted with President Ezer Weizman, Prime Minister Ehud Barak, Minister for 
Regional Co-operation Shimon Peres, Deputy Minister of Defence Ephriam Sneh, and 
Police and Security agencies. The tour was undertaken with the main focus on problems of 
trans-border terrorism. Israel and India have both grappled with it during the last two 
decades. Terrorist organisations are now known to establish and have international 
linkages which makes it necessary for victim countries to learn from the experience of 
and work in close co-operation with each other in the interest of promotion of peace and 
progress and suppression of terrorism. 
The visit has opened up the possibility of increased technological, technical and 
intelligence co-operation between India and Israel. The two sides have agreed to work 
for early establishment of a Joint Working Group between the two countries. 
The visit, which is a part of the ongoing high-level exchanges between the two 
countries, has had no effect on India's traditional ties of friendship and cooperation with the 
Arab countries. Our relations with the Arab world continue to remain substantive, 
multifaceted and wide ranging.

power mainly due to weather beating loads resulting in low voltage in Delhi system. 
Under such critical conditions of low voltage and low frequency, DVB has to resort to 
unscheduled load shedding for the security of its own system and the Northern Grid as a 
whole. En order to mitigate the shortages during summer of 2000, an Action Plan was 
drawn up in November, 1999 for meeting power demand in NCT Delhi. The Action 
Plan envisaged steps for preventive maintenance of generating units, allocation of 
adequate supply of Naphtha and HSD for gas power plants sourcing power supply to 
Delhi, enhancement of allocation to Delhi from 15% unallocated quota to 25%, supply 
of power by HPSEB under bilateral arrangement, strengthening of transmission and 
distribution system in Delhi, preventive  maintenance of tran smission lines/sub-
stations, installation of shunt capacitors etc. and also maximising generation from 
centra! power stations located in the Northern Region etc. The implementation of the 
Action Plan was discussed in December, 1999 and reviewed in May, 2000 in the 
Ministry of Power with all concerned including Delhi Vidyut Board and Government 
of NCT of Delhi. 
(d) Does not arise, in view of (b) and (c) above.

427. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister of

129

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) The Government is in receipt of the Confederation of 
Indian Industries (CII) report on Independent Power Producers (IPPs). 
(b) and (c) The reasons for adequate domestic or foreign investment not fructifying 
in the power sector is not lack of a clear and transparent policy, but various other factors, 
primary among which is the poor financial health of most of the State Electricity Boards 
who do not have the fi nancial capability to s upport more than a few projects in terms of 
regular payment of bills of electricity purchased by them from IPPs. The poor financial 
health of the State Electricity Boards and the insistence by lenders on strong payment 
security packages has been the main problem in the private power projects achieving 
financial closure. With a view to findi ng a solution to this problem and to 
simplify/decentralise the procedure for clearance of private power projects and to 
attract more investment in the power sect or, the Government ha s already initiated 
several measures which include:—  
—  minimising the number of clearances required to be obtained for the purpose 
of appraisal of the private power projects by Central Electricity Authority 
(CEA). 
—  minimising the role of the Foreign Investment Promotion Board by providing 
for automatic approval for foreign equity in selected categories and 
enlarging the provisions for automatic approval for such projects and 
liberalisation of the Foreign Direct Investment regime by removal of the upper 
limit for foreign direct investment in respect of projects relating to electric 
generation, transmission and distributi on (other than atomic reactor power 
plants). 
—  delegating more powers for environmental clearance to State Governments. 
—  raising the financial limits for power projects which require the clearance 
from CEA. 
—  preparation of a shelf of projects to facilitate early execution and reduction 
of time required for implementation. 
—  close monitoring at various levels to expedite clearances, remove bottlenecks 
and to resolve the 'last mile' problems in achieving financial closure.

—  The Electricity Laws Amendment, Act, 1998 was enacted to make

—  A policy on Hydro Power Development has been initiated for accelerating

electric potential at faster pace, incr ease the private investment and promote

430. SHRI R.P. GOENKA; Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state:

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The losses being incurred by various State 
Governments on account of power theft are. not being separately assessed. However, 
the experience of States undergoing reforms indicate that the losses on account of T & 
D, theft and pilferage are to the extent of 45% of the power generated. A rough 
estimate indicate that out of the total energy generated only 55% is billed (Rs. 62,000 
crores). Of the amount not billed 20% loss is sustained due to theft and pilferate (Rs. 
22,500 crores). 
A statement showing the percentage T & D losses including both the technical and 
commercial losses as assessed by the concerned State Electricity Boards/Electricity 
Departments for the Year 1997-98 is annexed (See below) 
Quantum jump in the T & D losses reported by the reforming states is apparently 
on the account of the ability of the vertica lly integrated SEBs to misclassify losses. 
This would not be possible in restructur ed generation, transmission and distribution 
utilities. Restructured distribution entities would be under compulsion to assess the 
losses nearer to actuals. 
(c) and (d) Though the power distribu tion falls within the purview of the  State 
Governments and the activities pertaining to prevention of theft of electricity and 
removing illegal connection have  to be taken care of by the power utilities operating 
under their jurisdiction. Theft of electricity has been made a cognizable offence under 
the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, and the utilities have to  effectively implement the 
provisions of the law to curb the theft of electricity. 
In the Common Minimum National Action Plan for power announced in

period of 2 years. 
3. All electric supplies should be metered by 2002 AD.  
4. Compulsory annual energy audit to be ensured in respect of large consumers of 
more than 100 KVA load. 
5. Time of the day metering would be introduced for big power consumers for better 
load management.

T & D losses by energy audit, 100% metering, reduction of power theft and

(c) the quantum of power to be made available at the rate of cost of production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes Sir; in terms of the approved formula for sharing of power 
from Central Sector Hydel Stations, 12% power is to be supplied free of cost to those 
States of the Region (including the State where the hydroelectric project is located) 
where distress by way of submergence/dislocation of population is caused by setting up 
the project. The Allocation to the State in which the project is located where the entire 
distress takes place is 12 percent. If the distress affects more than one State then the 
allocation is made in proportion to the extent of distress. 
(b) The project authorities, na mely, Nathpa Jhakri Power Corporation (NJPC) has 
estimated that the annual revenue available to Himachal Pradesh by the sale of free 
power would be about Rs. 2.04.57 crores based on the tariff of Rs. 2.57 per unit for the 
first year of operation. 
(c) In terms of provisions contained in Articles of Association of NJPC, after supply 
of 12% power free of cost to Himachal Pradesh, the balance (88%) of power from 
Nathpa Jhakri H.E. Project (1500 MW) would be distributed at bus bar rates as under:— 
(i)25% of the remaining &8% of gene rated power shall be allocated to 
Government of Himachal Pradesh in lieu of 25% cost sharing of the project by 
Government of Himachal Pradesh. 
(ii) the remaining 66% of generated power shall be at the disposal of the 
Government of India in lieu of 75% of cost sharing of the project by the 
Government of India and shall be allocated by the Government of India to 
various States of the region (including Himachal Pradesh) in accordance with 
the approved formula.

DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SUBHASH MAHARIA): (a) to (c) Jawahar Rozgar Yojana 
(JRY) was introduced w.e.f. 1.4.1989. The scheme was implemented throughout the 
country including Arunachal Pradesh except Union Territories of Chandigarh and 
Delhi. The scheme was specifically meant for rural areas and not for towns and cities. 
The objectives of the programme was to provide additional gainful wage employment 
to the rural poor. The programme also aimed at creation of sustained employment by 
strengthening rural economic infrastructure besides creating community and social 
assets for the direct and continuing benefits of the rural poor. Forestry and Horticulture 
were permissible activities under the scheme. The funds under the scheme were utilized 
by the district panchayat, intermediate level panchayat and village panchayat in the 
ratio of 15:15:70 respectively. These institutions were allowed to take up any work as 
per their share of funds and the felt needs of the area. Village-wise details of the works 
undertaken were not monitored at the Central level. 
The erstwhile JRY has been restructured, streamlined and renamed as Jawahar Gram 
Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) w i t h  effect from 1.4.99. The primary objective of the 
programme is to create dema nd driven village infrastr ucture. The programme is 
implemented by the village panchayat with the approval of Gram Sabha. Forestry and 
Horticulture continue to remain permissible activities under the JGSY.

463. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the implementation of the Technology 
Upgradation Fund Scheme for Textile and Jute industries; 
(b) if so, the details thereof;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) The Government have 
constituted a 22 members Inter-Ministerial Steering Committee (IMSC), under the 
Chairmanship of Secretary (Textiles), for reviewing and monitoring the implementation 
of the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) for the textile and jute industries. 
The IMSC has been reviewing and monitoring the implementation of TUFS on a regular 
basis, and has so far held 5 meetings. It is an ongoing exercise. On the basis of feed-back 
received from various quarters, the IMSC has reviewed the scheme and taken a number of 
decisions for effective implementation of the scheme. The important decisions taken are 
as under: 
(i) The loans which were sanctioned prior to 1-4-1999; but not disbursed can be 
considered under TUFS as fresh cases, if otherwise they meet the parameters 
of TUFS. 
(ii) In case a part disbursed loans, if the borrower wishes to be considered for 
TUFS benefits, a fresh project conforming to TUFS norms can be submitted 
to the lending agency after terminating the existing loan cases. 
(iii) In respect of Captive Power Generation, ceiling on investment has 
been relaxed. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [26 July, 2000] 
(iv) The energy s a v i n g  devices, effluent treatment p l a n ts  and water treatment 
plants can be installed without any ceiling on investment. 
(v) The preliminary and pre-operative expenses and incremental margin money on 
working capital have been included as eligible investment under the scheme. 
(vi) Yarn processing has been made an additional eligible downstream value 
addition activity for investment in capacity expansion in cotton ring spinning 
mills. 
(vii) The maximum expired life (vintage) of certain second hand machinery has 
been enhanced from 5 years to 10 years. 
(viii)Semi-automatic looms are now allowed for decentralised powerloom sector. 
(ix) Air jet looms of 165 cms. width (capable of manufacturing 60 inch width Grey 
fabrics) and similar width in case of Water Jet looms and also automatic 
shuttle looms are eligible under TUFS.

applications with a total project cost of Rs. 7668 crore were received. Out of them,

Rs. 904 crore has been disbursed against 232 applications 
(d) and (e) A number of representations have been received from various quarters 
for relaxation in financial norms of the nodal/co-opted financial agencies. Representations 
have been duly considered, and important decisions taken in this regard are as under:

continuous profit for availing of loan for the units which are viable, having 
good track record with a positive net worth even though they had incurred 
losses.

other cases. IDBI agreed to relax it even upto 17.5% in extremely deserving 
cases.

Residential permits for refugees in Delhi 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa); Madam, India is one of the 
countries in the world with largest number of refugees. At this moment, in 
India, there are about one lakh Tibetans and another one lakh Sri Lankan 
refugees. In addition, there are also about 20,000 refugees in the capital city 
of Delhi, out of which about 15.000 are Afghans and the rest are Burmese. 
Somalis. Sudanese, Iranians and some others. The majority of Afghan 
refugees are Hindus and Sikhs of Indian origin. In addition to refugees from 
foreign countries, we also have a large number of internalry displaced persons 
from Kashmir and the North-Eastern region, who suffer a similar plight. There 
is presently no law in India to deal with the refugee situation. Such a law is 
essential to prevent arbitrariness, ad-hocism and abuse of power at lower 
levels of bureaucratic decision-making. An Eminent Persons Group, 
including former Chief Justice of India, Justice P.N. Bhagwati, submitted last 
year to the Government of India a draft Refugees and Asylum Seekers 
Protection Act, 2000." Our own colleague, the former Chief Justice of India, 
Shri Ranganath Misra, played an important role in this respect when he was 
the Chairman of the Human Rights Commission. As per this Act, persons 
who are guilty of crimes against humanity, drug trafficking, acts of terrorism 
or are members of political groups banned in India, are not entitled to 
refugee status. The Government should bring this legislation before 
Parliament, and in the meanwhile, even if the Government does not want to 
put a legislation as 
190 

[26 JULY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
such, a Manual of Practices and Procedures on refugee matters for the use 
of the administration dealing with the subject,, should be immediately 
prepared and finalized. It is also necessary to provide immediately 
residential permits to all refugees who have been accepted in India, 
particularly in urban areas like Delhi, in the interest of national security and 
in the interest of refugees themselves. Thank you.

SHRI B. P. SINGHAL (Uttar Pradesh): Madam Deputy Chairperson, this 
Bill is an amendment to the parent Act, and that parent Act deals with the 
disposal of the property of those who have been declared as deserters or 
who have died a natural death or, otherwise, who are not there any more. The 
parent Act was enacted to see to it that the entire responsibility of paying all 
the dues that belonged to an Army or an Air Force personnel devolved on 
the Commanding Officer; that duty was devolved on the Commanding 
Officer to collect that amount and then have it paid to the heirs whose names 
were already mentioned in the officer's service record. Now, why is this 
amount sought to be increased? In 1954, when I joined the IPS, my salary 
was Rs.350/-. At that time, a constable's or a jawan's salary used to be so 
low that the total cumulative gratuity, PF, did not, perhaps, come to even Rs. 
10,0007-. Today, the salaries have gone up and, naturally, all-these amounts will 
be much more. So, in keeping with that, the limit has been increased to Rs.2 
lakhs and I hope that this limit wiil be sufficient to take care of most of them. 
Hon. Member, Shri Pachouri, raised a very relevant point about war-widows. 
But, that is a totally different subject. We know from Press reports that the 
Army is already seized of the issue, about the kind of problems that parents 
are experiencing or even the wives are experiencing. I think they are 
evolving some methods to ensure that the money is given to the members of 
the family of the diseased. In the title of the Bill also, the word '2000' needs 
to be added. The hon. Minister is, of course, moving an amendment in this 
regard. The only point here was about the change of names of Acts because, 
technically, the word used is 1913' of the Administrator General's Act; it was 
amended in 1963; therefore, it was changed to 1963. Similarly, the Indian 
Lunacy Act, 1912, was amended to become the Mental Health

this Bill as it is. In the Statement of Objects and Reasons it has been 
mentioned, "any person appearing to such authority to be entitled to such 
property and money, without requiring the production of any probate, letter of 
administration, succession certificate or other such conclusive evidence of 
title." Madam, here comes the problem. There is no doubt that this Bill has 
been brought with a laudable object to avoid expenses and troublesome and 
time-consuming procedure. But the difficulties and problems which are going 
-to be faced have also to be taken into consideration while passing this Bill, 
Under the Army Act, nomination by an Army person is provided. An Army 
person can nominate anybody to receive his assets. Now, nominee need not 
necessarily be a Segal heir. Nominee does not necessarily mean all the 
legal heirs. Only one person can be nominated. , He may be or may not be a 
legal heir. Under the Insurance Act, the position is that the nominee is only a 
legal agent. He has to collect the amount and distribute it to the legal heirs. 
Now, that provision itself has to be taken into consideration. Madam, under 
the Hindu Succession Act, wife, son, daughter and mother are the legal heirs 
of a Hindu. But if a nomination is made in favour of a particular person and

heirs, then what will be the position? As a matter of fact, in our place North

taken any steps to help them who were in dire straits. The parents also said 
that Poongavanam had threatened them with dire consequences if they 
came for help to her."   Madam, this is the situation.

THE COTTON CLOTH (REPEAL) BILL, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES {SHRI KASHIRAM RANA): Madam, I 
beg to move: 
"That the Bill to repeal the Cotton Cloth Act, 1918, as passed by 
Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration . 
Madam, the Cotton Cloth Act was enacted in 1918, with a view to 
encouraging and maintaining the supply of standard cotton cloth 
manufactured in the country, at reasonable rates, to the weaker sections of 
society. This Act, has jurisidction to the whole of India. Under the Act, the 
State Governments are empowered to appoint a Controller for 
implementation of its provisions and also an Advisory Committee to assist 
the Controller. The State Governments are also empowered to fix the price 
of the standard cloth, prescribing the authority for grant of licences for sale 
of standard cloth and rute-making power for giving effect to the provisions of 
the Act. The Controller so appointed, is empowered to make general or 
special orders for manufacture, transport, distribution and sale or purchase 
of cotton cloth.   The Controller is also empowered to fix the 
221 

RAJYA. SABHA [26 JULY, 2000] 
price to be paid to the manufacturer, to declare and define the classes of 
standard cloth, etc. This Act also has provisions for imposing penalties for its 
contravention with imprisonment up to 6 months or with fine or with 
both. 
Over the years, the textile industry has been growing steadily. The 
production of cloth from 1980-81 to 1999-2000 has risen by an estimated 
200 per cent at an average annual growth rate of about 6%. The per capita 
availability of cloth, which was 17.30 sq. mt. during 1980-81, rose to 28.19 
sq. mt. during 1998-99 an increase of about 63 per cent showing an average 
growth of 2.75 per cent. Apart from meeting the ever increasing domestic 
need, the export of cotton textiles alone rose from Rs. 400 crore in 1981-82 
to about Rs. 18,000 crore in 1999-2000. 
It is our endeavour to develop a strong and vibrant textile industry 
that can produce cloth of good quality at reasonable prices, which meets the 
growing needs of the people and also contributes to the economic growth of 
the nation while competing with confidence for an increasing share of the 
global market. For this purpose, the Government has taken several steps. 
The Technology Upgradation Funds Scheme (TUFS), that is in operation 
from 1,4.1999 for modernisation of the Textiles and Jute Industries, and the 
Technology Mission of Cotton Development are some such important 
initiatives. 
The Government of India had enacted the Essential Commodities 
Act in 1955. Cotton and textiles are essential commodities under the 
provisions of this Act. In exercise of the powers conferred upon it by Section 
3 of the Essential Commodities Act, Government of India has issued the 
Textile (Development & Regulation ) Order, 1993, which is comprehensive 
and generally covers all the provisions of Cotton Cloth Act, 1918. While the 
Cotton Cloth Act, 1918 deals with only one category viz. Cotton Cloth, the 
Textile (Development & Regulation ) Order 1993, deals with all types of 
cloth, yarn and other textiles. This order is implemented by the Textile 
Commissioner, who is appointed by the Government of India and has 
jurisdiction over entire India. Due to the fact that, man-made fibre textiles 
were not in vogue in 1918, the scope and focus of the Cotton Cloth Act has 
been extremely narrow. Therefore, in the present scenario, the Act is 
superfluous, redundant and irrelevant and deserves to be repealed.

The Cabinet has approved the proposal for repeal of the Cotton 
Cloth Act. 1918. The Commission of Review of Administrative Laws has 
also recommended the repeal of this Act. 
The Lok Sabha passed the Cotton Cloth (Repeal) Bill, 2000 on 5 th 
May, 2000. I request the House to approve the Cotton Cloth (Repeal) Bill, 
2000 as passed by the Lok Sabha. 
The question was proposed. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: We will pass the Bill. There is no 
problem. I will call Shardaji to make her speech, but before she makes her 
speech, t would like to bring to your notice, Mantriji, that you are repealing a 
redundant Bill. Fine. But the situation in respect of the cotton yarn is not 
very good, as far as the handloom people are concerned. Their condition is 
very bad. Some people in Andhra Pradesh are on the verge of committing 
suicide. Even some place in U.P. and in Maharashtra, where they are using 
cotton, while the cotton prices are crashing, the bunkars are not getting 
enough cotton yarn. While you ask us to repeal it, without discussion, from 
the Chair, I am telling you, on behalf of the entire House, which is 
concerned about these people, that khadi is becoming redundant. So, all 
these things you must take into consideration. We assure you that we wilt 
pass the Bill. Why don't you give us some assurance on that, that you will 
take care of the bunkars in the country?

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
New Uplinking Policy 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam, earlier, satellite TV 
channels were not permitted to uplink their programmes from India. 
However, as the hon. Members would recollect, satellite based TV channels 
have started beaming their programmes into India by uplinking their 
channels from hubs abroad since early nineties, as the satellite technology 
has become available. As a result, they have remained outside the Indian 
jurisdiction. In order to bring them back under the purview of the Indian laws, 
the uplinking policy was relaxed for the first time on 9.6.1998 and the Indian 
broadcastsg companies with a minimum of 80% Indian share holding and  
Indian management  control were permitted to 
 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [26 JULY, 2000] 
uplink their channels from India but only through VSNL. This permission was 
restricted to only those Indian companies, which were being released foreign 
exchange for uplinking from abroad. The policy was further liberalised on 
26.3.1999 and all Indian companies which were broadcasters, with a 
minimum 80% Indian share holding and Indian management control were 
permitted to uplink their channels through their own earth station as well. 
The Cabinet in its meeting on 25.7.2000 has decided to further 
liberalise the uplinking policy. As per the new policy, an Indian company, 
which need not be a braodcaster, will be permitted, subject to necessary 
security clearance, to set up uplinking hub or teleport facilities for purposes 
of hiring it out to broadcasters. Permissible foreign equity in such companies 
will be the same as in case of telecom sector, which is persently 49%, 
inclusive of NRI/OCB investments with Indian management control. These 
companies will be permitted to uplink only those TV channels which would 
be specifically approved or permitted by the Government. All TV channels, 
irrespective of their equity holding, ownership or management control will be 
permitted to uplink their programmes from India, subject to necessary 
security clearance, provided they undertake to comply with our broadcasting 
codes. This new policy will not only bring a large number of TV channels 
within the discipline of our broadcasting codes but will also generate 
substantial employment opportunities as India becomes an important hub 
offering state of the art facilities for uplinking. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA) in the Chair] 
Our news agencies have been seriousry handicapped vis-a-vis 
their foreign counterparts as they have been deprived the use of the latest 
technology of Satellite News Gathering (SNG) for purposes of news 
gathering and their further distribution. Because of this handicap, the news 
disseminated by Indian News Agencies reaches the electronic and print 
media late and in the intervening period, contrary point of vie"w remains 
unchallenged in the world media. The new uplinking policy of the 
Government would remove this handicap and permit uplinking facility to the 
Indian News agencies for news gathering and its further distribution to other 
news agencies/broadcasters. For this purpose, Indian news agencies would 
mean those incorporated in India and accredited by the Press 
232 

[26 JULY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Information Bureau and 100% owned by Indians with Indian management 
control. This will give the Indian news agencies the much desired 
competitive edge over the foreign news agencies. 
As in case of earlier policy, such uplinking facilities will be 
permitted with both Indian and foreign satellites. However, proposals 
envisaging Indian satellites will be accorded preferential treatment.
